oneLiner: eClerx does the specialised back-office grind big banks would rather not touch, and it does it brilliantly: growing 22%, earning 35% on capital. Yet the stock has de-rated, because it gets paid by the head, and AI is coming for exactly that kind of work.

verdict.keyQuestion: The operator is superb. Does AI erode the per-head model faster than the pivot to value-added work can grow?

facts.snapshot: eClerx is an Indian outsourcing firm that runs specialised back-office operations for others: trade processing for big banks, plus content and marketing work for media, telecom and luxury brands, delivered mostly from India.

overview: When an investment bank has to process millions of derivative trades, or a luxury brand needs thousands of product photos edited and tagged for its website, that work is repetitive, fiddly, and expensive to do in-house. eClerx is the company you hand it to. It runs the unglamorous but essential back office for big financial firms, telecom and media companies, and retail and luxury brands. For most of its life it charged by the person: you need 100 trained people running trade support, eClerx hires, trains and manages them from India at a fraction of the onshore cost. That per-person model built a business earning 35% on capital. It is also the exact model AI now threatens, because AI is a rising tide and repetitive human work is the ground eClerx stands on. That is the whole argument around the stock.

editorial.realBusiness: eClerx is not a software company. It rents out trained brains at India prices, doing the specialised grunt work banks and brands would rather not keep in-house.
editorial.whyExists: Big banks and brands sit on oceans of repetitive, specialised operations work, trade processing, data management, product content, that is too costly and too distracting to run themselves. eClerx earns its place by doing that work cheaper, faster, and with real domain training, above all in the messy plumbing of financial-markets operations.
editorial.whyNotAlreadyWon: Because the work is embedded and specialised. Once eClerx's people learn a bank's tangled internal systems and quirks, moving that work somewhere else is risky, so clients stay put. That stickiness is the moat. It is also, awkwardly, the very thing AI could wash away, because the moat guards work that is getting easier to automate.

editorial.whyNow: The stock fell about 14% over the past year while profit grew 30%, so the multiple squeezed from the high-20s down toward 23x. This year's numbers are not the worry. What the market is pricing is what AI does to the model over the next several years, and that argument is laid out in the AI fork below. If the market is overrating the damage AI does, the lower multiple could turn out cheap. If the economics really are eroding, it may not be cheap enough.
editorial.remember: eClerx is a superb operator standing on ground the tide is coming for. Judge it on whether AI becomes its tool or its undoing, not on this quarter's margin.

ipoFlag: No repackaging games. eClerx listed in 2007 and has traded for well over a decade. It did do a 1:1 bonus issue in March 2026, which doubles the share count and halves the per-share price optically but changes nothing about the business or your ownership.

moneyFlow.spread: The gap between what the client would pay onshore and what eClerx spends to deliver from India is the arbitrage spread. That spread, not software, is the gross engine of the whole company.

aiFork.premise: AI will almost certainly cut the human effort this work takes. The real question is not whether, but who pockets the value that the cut creates.
aiFork.trigger: AI arrives → human effort per task falls

branches.label: eClerx captures the value
outcomes: Charges for the outcome, not headcount

aiFork.takeaway: So that is the thing to work out: when AI makes the work easier, does eClerx keep the gain, or does the client take it?

counterpoint.heading: What if AI makes outsourcing more valuable, not less?
counterpoint.body: The bear case assumes AI shrinks the work. It might instead change it. Banks will not obviously need fewer outsourced operations in an automated world; they may just need different ones. As workflows get automated, someone still has to build the systems, watch them, catch what they get wrong, and run the whole thing. If eClerx moves from supplying people to owning that workflow, the value it captures per client could rise even as the number of people it deploys falls.
counterpoint.caveat: This is a possibility, not a forecast. eClerx has to prove it in the revenue mix and the economics, not in the concall. Management saying it is one thing; it showing up in the numbers is another.

scorecard.intro: You do not have to guess which way the fork breaks. These are the numbers that tell you, quarter by quarter, whether eClerx is capturing the AI gain or losing it to clients.

scorecard.note: eClerx does not disclose all of these cleanly each quarter, so read the trend across the ones it does. Revenue per employee is the single clearest window into whether the economics are moving away from pure headcount.

business.unitOfRevenue: Historically, one billed person. Think of hiring a team: a client says it needs, say, 200 trained people to run its trade-support desk, and eClerx supplies and manages them from India at a rate per head well below the onshore cost. It is now shifting some of this toward outcome-based pricing, where it charges for a result delivered instead of heads deployed.
business.revenueModel: Mostly staff-based (per-person) contracts today, migrating toward outcome-based and productised deals. These are recurring, multi-year client relationships, not one-off projects.

segments.name: Financial Markets operations
segments.marginProfile: The specialist core. Derivatives and trade operations for banks. Sticky, higher-value.

segments.name: Digital / Customer Operations

segments.name: Analytics & Automation
segments.marginProfile: The growth bet, now a ~USD 90m book. Higher-value, AI-adjacent.

business.revenuePerUnitTrend: Two forces pull against each other. Indian wage inflation pushes eClerx's cost per person up, while clients push billing rates down, often using AI-driven productivity as the argument for a cheaper deal (management calls this deflationary pressure). eClerx's answer is to climb the value chain into analytics, automation, and outcome-based contracts where it is paid for results, not seats. Whether that climb outruns the deflation in the seat business is the single most important thing to watch. The segment percentages elsewhere are approximate reads of the mix, not exact disclosures.

industry.structure: Fragmented and competitive. Many BPM and KPO players, from global majors to niche specialists.
industry.competitors: Global majors like Accenture, Genpact and WNS are bigger and broader. Firstsource and Zensar are closer listed comparisons. eClerx competes on domain depth, especially in financial-markets operations, rather than scale.
industry.pricingPower: Medium and under pressure. Domain expertise gives some pricing hold in the financial-markets niche, but clients are actively pushing for AI-led cost savings across the industry.
industry.demandDriver: The desire of large firms to offload repetitive, specialised operations work at lower cost. That driver is structural, but the form it takes (people versus software) is changing.
industry.driverType: Structural (outsourcing is not going away) but with a technology shift (AI) reshaping how the work gets done and priced.
industry.tam: Large global BPM and outsourcing market growing at high single digits, but the value is migrating from headcount-based delivery toward automation and outcome-based models.
industry.penetration: Outsourcing is well established; growth here is share-gain and moving up the value chain, not a greenfield land grab.
industry.valueChainPosition: The outsourced operations layer sitting behind a client's own systems. Valuable while the work is human-intensive, exposed if that work automates away.

business.qualityVerdict: As an operator, eClerx is genuinely excellent: ~22% revenue growth, ~35% ROCE, tiny capital needs, and cash flow that tracks profit. The niche in financial-markets operations is real and sticky. There is very little to fault in how the company is run. The hard question is not about the operator at all. It is whether the pivot to higher-value work outruns the pressure on the per-person model, and that is a separate matter the two-engine read and the summary take up.

cashFlowNote: This is a clean cash machine. Operating cash flow beats reported profit, capex is tiny (about Rs 132 cr on Rs 4,000+ cr of revenue) because a services business needs desks and laptops, not factories, and free cash flow of Rs 756 cr in FY26 is comfortably positive. Debtor days at 59 are normal for IT services, where clients pay on monthly billing cycles. There is no accounting worry here. The profit is real and it turns into cash. The risk in this business is strategic (AI), not financial.

growth.label: Q1 FY27 PAT
growth.hint: +16% YoY, ~7% down QoQ on wage hikes

management: Founder-led by PD Mundhra and Anjan Malik, who built eClerx from 2000 and still anchor the promoter group (about 54.5%, with zero pledge). The record is an operator's: two decades of high-return, cash-generative growth without diluting shareholders or piling on debt. The test in front of them now is the hardest of their careers, steering a company through an AI shift that threatens the per-person model it was built on. To their credit, they are meeting it in the open on concalls, naming the deflationary pressure, moving toward outcome-based and non-FTE deals, and building the analytics and automation book. So far they look like people addressing the problem rather than waving it off. Judge them over the next few years by one thing: whether the value-added mix grows faster than the seat business shrinks.

sources: Domain depth in financial-markets and derivatives operations
Embedded processes inside client systems (switching cost)
moat.note: The moat is real but narrow, and it is being tested. eClerx's edge is knowing a client's messy operations so intimately that moving the work is risky, plus genuine specialism in derivatives processing that generic outsourcers lack. That has held clients for years. Here is the caveat, and it is about the direction the moat does not face: AI does not beat eClerx on service. It shrinks how much human work there is to bill for. The 'shrinking island' lens below unpacks that. Narrow, real today, and on notice.

narrative: eClerx has compounded quietly for two decades: revenue from Rs 2,160 cr in FY22 to Rs 4,117 cr in FY26, profit from Rs 418 cr to Rs 706 cr, all on tiny capital and essentially net cash (D/E 0.17). FY26 was a strong year, revenue up ~22% and profit up ~30%, capped with a 1:1 bonus issue. And yet the stock fell about 14% over the year. The reason is not in the results; it is in the theme. eClerx sits in the corner of IT most directly in AI's path, the outsourcing of repetitive human work, and the market spent the year marking down anything that bills by the hour or the head. So a business that grew earnings 30% watched its multiple shrink instead of stretch.
risks: AI disruption of the core model. eClerx is paid largely for human effort on repetitive work, which is exactly what AI automates. If clients use AI to cut headcount-based spend faster than eClerx moves to outcome-based revenue, growth and margins compress. High.
Margin pressure. Indian wage inflation pushes costs up while clients push billing rates down (deflationary pressure). Margins have drifted and can drift further. Medium-High.
Client concentration. Top-10 clients are about 59% of revenue. Losing or shrinking one large relationship would hurt. Medium.
Competition from larger players. Accenture, Genpact and WNS have deeper resources to build AI-led delivery and undercut on price. Medium.
Currency. Revenue is largely in USD against India costs, so a sharp rupee move swings reported margins. Medium.

summary: eClerx pairs high growth (22%), high returns (35% ROCE), a net-cash balance sheet, and clean cash flow, and after a 14% fall while earnings rose 30% it trades at about 23x. Those two facts sit uneasily together. The reason is the labour-arbitrage model: AI is built to compress exactly the human-effort billing eClerx lives on. Management is pivoting to analytics, automation, and outcome deals, and eClerx is too good an operator to wave away, but whether the pivot outruns the pressure is genuinely unknown. The old model clearly works today. Whether it keeps working once the work itself gets easier to automate is the open question, and the next few quarters of revenue mix, revenue per employee, and pricing should start to answer it. This is not a buy or sell call. Do your own work and talk to a SEBI-registered adviser.

engine.earnings: The earnings engine is running well and it is cash-backed: FY26 profit up ~30%, TTM profit growth ~28%, ROCE ~35%, and free cash flow that tracks profit. Q1 FY27 (June 2026) is the near-term wobble, and it lives in one line: revenue rose ~24% YoY to Rs 1,152 cr, but profit of Rs 164 cr grew only 16% YoY and slipped about 7% QoQ, as the April wage hike and new delivery centres (Lima live, Cairo starting) pushed EBITDA margin to 24.2% and PAT margin to 14%. Growth is fine. The squeeze is on margin, which is exactly the tension this report keeps flagging. From here, the catalyst is the analytics and automation book (now ~USD 90m) scaling up; the drag is pricing deflation.
engine.multiple: The multiple has already compressed. Over the past year profit grew ~30% while the stock fell ~14%, so the PE slid from the high-20s toward 23x. That is the market pricing AI risk, not a business miss. At 23x for a 35%-ROCE, debt-free compounder, the multiple is not demanding by its own history, but it is not a giveaway either, given the structural question hanging over it.
engine.verdict: On the mechanics, earnings are rising, the multiple has compressed, and returns are stable. That combination creates room for a re-rating, but only if the market's AI worry proves overdone. This is not the clean setup it would be for a company with no structural threat: the compression reflects a real, unresolved question about whether the revenue itself is durable. So the upside is genuine but conditional on the AI transition going well. The evidence to watch is whether the value-added mix grows fast enough to offset the pressure on the seat-based business.

lenses.name: The price fell while earnings rose
lenses.reading: Profit grew about 30% in FY26 but the stock fell about 14%, so the multiple compressed rather than expanded, while ROE held near 29% the whole way. In a business with no structural threat, that would be a clean re-rating setup, cheaper stock, same quality. Here the compression is the market pricing the AI question. So read it as conditional, not free.

lenses.name: A moat around a shrinking island
lenses.reading: eClerx's stickiness comes from doing embedded, repetitive work nobody wants to move. But AI does not attack head-on; it attacks the ground. It does not beat eClerx on service, it shrinks how much human work is left to bill for. A moat is only worth as much as the thing it protects, and here that thing, the island, is being eaten from underneath.

lenses.name: Loyalty measured before the alternative existed
lenses.reading: Years of high client retention were earned in a world where the only real option was human-run offshore delivery. AI is the first genuine alternative to that model. So the loyalty record tells you clients were sticky when there was no substitute. It tells you much less about how sticky they stay once one finally exists.

lenses.name: Operator meeting the threat head-on
lenses.reading: This is the hopeful side. Management is not dodging the AI question on concalls; it is naming the deflation, moving to outcome-based and non-FTE deals, and building the analytics book. That is what a good operator does. The thesis is not that the threat is fake. It is that this team may be good enough to steer through it. Judge them by the value-added mix, not the talk.
